newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran foreign minister in Saudi with Fahd invite.
newsitem.headline: Iran foreign minister in Saudi with Fahd invite.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati arrived in Saudi Arabia on Saturday with an invitation to King Fahd to visit Tehran, diplomatic sources said.
Velayati, on his first visit to the kingdom since 1993, was greeted in the capital Riyadh by his Saudi counterpart Prince Saud al-Faisal.
"For the time being relations between the two countries are somewhat better than before," the minister was quoted by Iran's state news agency IRNA as saying.
It said King Fahd was expected to receive the minister on Saturday night.

IRNA quoted Velayati as saying there was much room for broadening of the two countries' relations and necessary measures should be taken in this regard. He added that he would discuss Tehran-Riyadh relations during his stay.

Relations between Saudi Arabia, a Sunni-ruled pro-Western monarchy which is host to U.S. forces, and Iran, an Islamic republic whose Shi'ite leaders vehemently oppose American influence in the Gulf, are correct but cool.

Iranian media have called the visit highly significant and said it was likely to help ease tension in the strategic Gulf region, where the Saudis and their Gulf Arab allies have accused Tehran of interfering in their internal affairs.

The reason for Velayati's visit, part of a whistle-stop tour of 10 countries he began on March 9, is to deliver an invitation from President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani to King Fahd to visit Iran for a summit of the Moslem world's largest body.
The 51-nation Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), which is based in the Saudi commercial capital Jeddah, is due to hold its four-yearly summit in Tehran in December.
A Western diplomat in Tehran said Iranian leaders were worried about a possible lack of support because of an out-of-session summit timed to celebrate Pakistan's golden jubilee on March 23.
Gulf-based diplomats and analysts consider it highly unlikely that King Fahd would go to Tehran. But they said the invitation presented the Saudi royal family with a diplomatic dilemma.

The kingdom is home to two of Islam's most sacred shrines in the closed cities of Mecca and Medina. King Fahd styles himself Custodian of the Two Holy Shrines, emphasising his guardianship of the Moslem world's most revered places.
The king, or at the very least his half-brother Crown Prince Abdullah who often deputises for him, would be expected to attend the Moslem world's most important gathering, analysts said.
But the Saudis are less than pleased that Iran is about to take over the leadership of the OIC for the next four years.

"Even if there are not many heads of state in Tehran it would still be called a summit and the Iranians would still become chairman. This prospect is dreaded by the Saudis and their friends in the Gulf," a diplomatic source in the Iranian capital said earlier this week.
